Lets the military departments appoint claims commissions to settle claims by inhabitants of foreign countries for property loss, injury, or death caused by U.S. forces or incident to their noncombat activities abroad. The statute states its purpose as promoting and maintaining friendly relations through the prompt settlement of meritorious claims.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 55 Stat. 880](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/55/880){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 10 U.S.C. 2734](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/2734?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- 10 U.S.C. 2734(a): claims commissions may settle foreign claims for property loss, personal injury, or death caused by, or incident to noncombat activities of, the armed forces outside the United States.
- 10 U.S.C. 2734(b)(1): a claim must be presented within two years after it accrues.
- 10 U.S.C. 2734(b)(3): no claim may arise from enemy action or result directly or indirectly from combat by U.S. forces, apart from certain aircraft accidents or malfunctions.
- 10 U.S.C. 2734(d): for a meritorious claim above $100,000, the department may pay $100,000 and refer the rest to the Treasury for payment.

## Why it matters

The combat exclusion is the gap that shapes the rest of the civilian harm framework. People harmed in combat operations cannot claim under this act, so the military relied for decades on discretionary condolence payments and now on the statutory [ex gratia authority](ex-gratia-2019.qmd), which by its terms applies only where harm is not compensable under this act.

## Current status

In force. Restated in 1943 and codified in Title 10 in 1956. It does not cover harm caused by combat, which is why Congress later created a separate ex gratia authority.
